title: When Enzyme Results Mislead: Macroenzymes, Haemolysis and EDTA
summary: Separate true enzyme release from increased production, poor clearance by macroenzymes such as macroamylase, and in-tube artefacts: red-cell adenylate kinase falsely raising CK and EDTA contamination falsely lowering ALP and CK.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 21 Hit 3 (adenylate kinase and CK), Hit 4 (macroenzymes), Hit 10 (chelators), Trap 1 (macroamylasaemia), Trap 2 (EDTA tube) and Trap 5 (high enzyme is not always cell death). Checked against Thomas 2002, Fujisawa 2023, Dedeene 2023, Čásenská 2023, Dos Santos 2024, Lima-Oliveira 2014, Kalas 2021, Radišić Biljak 2025 and Leppäniemi 2019 (WSES). Hit 4 calls macroenzymes enzyme–autoantibody complexes with an IgG-like half-life; sources describe complexes with immunoglobulins (macroamylase mostly IgA), lipoproteins or self-polymers (register flag rv-macroenzyme-composition); the ~3-week half-life was not found and is not taught. Trap 2 names calcium as the CK cofactor, but the IFCC CK reagent contains EDTA to bind Ca2+ (register flag rv-ck-calcium-cofactor). Pending: the Oliver–Rosalki eponym, citrate/oxalate effects and calcium as a CK cofactor, GGT induction by ethanol, the renin exception, renal failure raising amylase/lipase, bile-salt release of ALP/GGT, “unmeasurably low” ALP. The IFCC CK method paper (Hørder 1990) had no machine-readable full text and its PDF was blocked, so it was not used.

objectives: List the routes that change serum enzyme activity: release, increased production, reduced clearance and in-vitro artefact.
Recognise the macroamylasaemia pattern and name the screening and confirmatory tests.
Explain how haemolysis falsely raises CK and how EDTA contamination falsely lowers ALP and CK.

scenes.title: Disease, or the sample?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three surprising enzyme results arrive on one shift — (1) a well outpatient with a visibly haemolysed specimen and a high CK; (2) a symptom-free adult whose amylase has been high for months while lipase is normal; (3) a chemistry specimen with a very low ALP that turns out to be contaminated with EDTA blood. Question token: “Disease, or the sample?”

cues.text: Three odd enzyme results arrive on one shift: a high creatine kinase in a haemolysed specimen from a well outpatient, and an amylase that has stayed high for months in someone with no symptoms and a normal lipase.
The third is a very low alkaline phosphatase in a chemistry specimen contaminated with blood from an EDTA tube.
Is each result telling you about disease, or about the sample?

scenes.title: Where serum enzyme activity comes from
scenes.altText: Schematic: a serum tube fed by three arrows. Card 1 “Release”: injured cells leak enzymes into blood. Card 2 “More production”: ALP is higher in children and adolescents because of osteoblast activity during bone growth. Card 3 “Slower clearance”: an enzyme bound into a large complex (a macroenzyme) is cleared poorly and accumulates. Card 4 “The assay”: routine enzyme measurements cannot distinguish a macroenzyme from the normal enzyme.

cues.text: A high serum enzyme does not always mean cell death. The first route is release: injured cells leak their enzymes into the blood.
The second route is more production. Alkaline phosphatase is higher in children and adolescents because of the osteoblast activity that comes with bone growth.
The third route is slower clearance. An enzyme bound into a large complex, a macroenzyme, is cleared poorly and builds up in the blood.
The analyser reports enzyme activity. Routine enzyme measurements cannot tell a macroenzyme from the normal enzyme, so the clinical pattern has to raise the suspicion.

scenes.title: Macroenzymes and macroamylasaemia
scenes.altText: Card “What a macroenzyme is”: a high-molecular-weight complex of an enzyme with immunoglobulin or lipoprotein, or a self-polymer; generally benign; reported prevalence under 0.1% to 3.5%; amylase and CK are the most common, but ALP, ALT, AST, GGT, LD and lipase are reported. Card “Macroamylase”: typically IgA (about 70%) and less often IgG (about 30%); renal clearance typically reduced 100-fold or more. Card “Pattern”: persistently high amylase, normal lipase, no pancreatic symptoms, normal renal function, urinary amylase not raised and a low amylase:creatinine clearance ratio. Card “Confirm”: polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation screen (%PPA above a laboratory-specific upper limit; one laboratory set 26% for amylase); gel filtration chromatography as gold standard; record the finding to avoid repeat investigations.

cues.text: A macroenzyme is a large complex: an enzyme bound to an immunoglobulin or a lipoprotein, or stuck to copies of itself. It is generally benign. Reported prevalence runs from under one in a thousand to a few percent, and amylase and creatine kinase are the most common.
Macroamylase is usually bound to IgA, about seventy percent, and less often to IgG. The complex is too big for efficient renal clearance, which typically falls a hundredfold or more.

So the pattern is a persistently high amylase with a normal lipase, no pancreatic symptoms and normal kidney function, while urinary amylase is not raised and the amylase to creatinine clearance ratio is low.

Polyethylene glycol precipitation is a quick first-line screen, judged against a laboratory-specific upper limit, and gel filtration chromatography is the gold standard. Document the finding so the patient is spared repeat investigations.

scenes.title: Two in-tube artefacts
scenes.altText: Card “Haemolysis and CK”: the reference CK method measures ATP formed from creatine phosphate and ADP (coupled through hexokinase and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase to NADPH at 340 nm); red cells are rich in adenylate kinase (AK1), which interconverts ATP + AMP and 2 ADP; released adenylate kinase raises enzymatically measured CK and CK-MB because the AMP and diadenosine pentaphosphate added to the reagent cannot fully inhibit it; haemolysis also raises LD and AST. Card “EDTA contamination”: EDTA chelates divalent ions (calcium, magnesium, zinc, manganese); in one study of lithium heparin specimens cited by Lima-Oliveira 2014, K3EDTA contamination lowered ALP by about 70%, CK by about 61% and amylase by about 34%, while AST and ALT were virtually unaffected; even 5% K2EDTA blood biased calcium, magnesium, potassium and LD. Hook answers: (1) haemolysis artefact, recollect; (2) suspect macroamylase; (3) EDTA contamination, recollect.

cues.text: Haemolysis can fake a high creatine kinase. The CK method measures the ATP it forms from ADP. Red cells are rich in adenylate kinase, which also turns two ADP into ATP and AMP, so it raises the measured CK and CK-MB.
CK reagents add AMP and diadenosine pentaphosphate to block adenylate kinase, but they cannot block it completely. Haemolysis also raises LD and AST.

EDTA chelates divalent ions such as calcium, magnesium and zinc. In one study of heparin plasma specimens, EDTA contamination cut alkaline phosphatase by about seventy percent and creatine kinase by about sixty, while AST and ALT were barely touched.
Back to the hook: recollect the haemolysed specimen, work up the high amylase for macroamylase, and recollect the EDTA-contaminated specimen.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “High enzyme = cell death” (✓ also more production or slower clearance, such as a macroenzyme); “High amylase + normal lipase = early pancreatitis” (✓ in a well patient with low clearance ratio, think macroamylase); “Haemolysis only matters for potassium” (✓ red-cell adenylate kinase falsely raises CK and CK-MB).

cues.text: Trap one: a high enzyme always means cells are dying. No: more production and slower clearance raise activity too.
Trap two: a high amylase with a normal lipase must be early pancreatitis. No: in a well patient with a low clearance ratio, think macroamylase.
Trap three: haemolysis only matters for potassium. No: red-cell adenylate kinase falsely raises creatine kinase and CK-MB.

scenes.title: Leak, Make, Stuck, Fake
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “LEAK, MAKE, STUCK, FAKE” — four ways a serum enzyme result goes up or down: LEAK from injured cells, MAKE more (bone ALP in growing children), STUCK in the blood (macroenzyme), FAKE in the tube (haemolysis adenylate kinase, EDTA chelation). Four tokens. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: leak, make, stuck, fake. Enzymes leak from injured cells, the body makes more, a complex gets stuck in the blood, or the tube fakes the result through haemolysis or EDTA.
Where it breaks: the routes can overlap, so a macroenzyme can sit alongside real disease; the size of an EDTA error depends on how much EDTA got in; and PEG limits must be set by each laboratory.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “High enzyme: leak, make more, or stuck (macroenzyme)”, “In the tube: haemolysis fakes high CK · EDTA fakes low ALP and CK”.

cues.text: Before calling an enzyme result disease, ask whether it is leakage, extra production, a poorly cleared macroenzyme, or an artefact in the tube such as haemolysis raising creatine kinase or EDTA lowering alkaline phosphatase.

props.label: High enzyme: leak · make more · stuck (macroenzyme)
In the tube: haemolysis → CK ↑ · EDTA → ALP ↓, CK ↓

explanation.what: Plain language: an enzyme number can go up because cells are injured, because the body makes more of the enzyme, because the enzyme is stuck to a large protein and the kidneys cannot clear it, or because something in the tube changed the reading. Scientific terms: macroenzyme, macroamylase (IgA/IgG complex), amylase:creatinine clearance ratio, polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation and percent PEG-precipitable activity (%PPA), gel filtration chromatography, adenylate kinase (AK1), diadenosine pentaphosphate, in-vitro haemolysis, EDTA chelation of divalent cations.
explanation.why: Routine assays report enzyme activity and cannot tell a macroenzyme from the normal enzyme. A complex too large for renal clearance accumulates; the reference CK method measures ATP formed from creatine phosphate and ADP (coupled via hexokinase and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase to NADPH at 340 nm), so red-cell adenylate kinase, which also makes ATP from ADP and is not fully suppressed by the inhibitors in the reagent, adds signal; EDTA chelates divalent metal ions such as magnesium, zinc and calcium.
explanation.measure: Macroamylasaemia: persistently raised amylase, normal lipase, no pancreatic symptoms, normal renal function, low amylase:creatinine clearance ratio; PEG screen against a laboratory-specific limit (26% PPA for amylase in one laboratory), gel filtration as gold standard. Haemolysis: raised CK and CK-MB (adenylate kinase), LD and AST. EDTA contamination: ALP about −70%, CK about −61%, amylase about −34% in one cited study; calcium, magnesium, potassium and LD biased from 5% K2EDTA blood.
explanation.differs: Release (injury) vs increased production (osteoblast ALP in growing children) vs reduced clearance (macroenzyme) vs in-vitro artefact; macroamylasaemia vs pancreatitis (lipase, symptoms, clearance ratio); haemolysis (falsely high CK) vs EDTA (falsely low ALP and CK).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a well patient with high amylase and normal lipase (macroamylasaemia), a haemolysed specimen with high CK (adenylate kinase), a very low ALP with low calcium and high potassium (EDTA contamination), or a question on why enzyme activity can rise without cell death.

mnemonic.text: LEAK, MAKE, STUCK, FAKE: enzymes LEAK from injured cells, the body MAKES more, a macroenzyme gets STUCK in the blood, or the tube FAKES it (haemolysis, EDTA).
mnemonic.explanation: Four routes to an abnormal serum enzyme result.
mnemonic.limitation: Routes overlap (a macroenzyme can coexist with disease); the size of an EDTA error depends on how much EDTA contaminated the specimen; PEG cut-offs are laboratory-specific.

analogyLimitations: Tube and complex drawings are schematic.
Percent changes come from one cited contamination study and vary with EDTA amount and method.
takeaway: Before calling an enzyme result disease, ask whether it is leakage, extra production, a poorly cleared macroenzyme, or an artefact in the tube such as haemolysis raising creatine kinase or EDTA lowering alkaline phosphatase.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with no abdominal symptoms has had serum amylase 2–3 times the upper limit for several months. Lipase and renal function are normal, and the amylase:creatinine clearance ratio is low. What is the most likely explanation?

options.rationale: Correct. A large amylase–immunoglobulin complex is poorly cleared by the kidney, so serum amylase stays high while lipase is normal and the clearance ratio is low.

Incorrect. Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed from two of three features: typical abdominal pain, amylase or lipase above three times the upper limit, and typical imaging. Lipase is the preferred marker; here lipase is normal and the patient is well.
Incorrect. Renal function is stated to be normal.
Incorrect. Haemolysis is a one-off specimen problem and does not explain months of high amylase with a low clearance ratio.

questions.stem: A visibly haemolysed specimen from a well outpatient shows a raised CK. Which mechanism best explains a falsely high result?

options.text: Red-cell adenylate kinase produces ATP from ADP in the reaction mixture, and the reagent inhibitors do not block it completely
options.rationale: Correct. Released adenylate kinase raises enzymatically measured CK and CK-MB.

options.text: Red cells contain large amounts of CK-MM
options.rationale: Incorrect. The documented interference is from red-cell adenylate kinase, not red-cell CK.

options.text: Haemoglobin chelates the magnesium the CK reaction needs
options.rationale: Incorrect. Chelation lowers activity and is the EDTA mechanism, not haemoglobin.

options.text: Haemolysis lowers renal clearance of CK
options.rationale: Incorrect. In-vitro haemolysis happens in the tube and has nothing to do with clearance.

questions.stem: A chemistry specimen shows very low calcium and magnesium, high potassium and an ALP far below the reference interval, while AST and ALT look normal. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Contamination of the specimen with EDTA
options.rationale: Correct. EDTA chelates divalent ions and adds potassium; contamination lowers ALP and CK while AST and ALT are barely affected.
Incorrect. Haemolysis raises potassium, LD and AST, but AST is normal here and haemolysis does not explain the very low calcium and magnesium.
Incorrect. Macroenzymes typically raise measured activity because clearance is reduced, and they would not lower calcium and magnesium.
Incorrect. Osteoblast activity raises ALP rather than lowering it.

claims.text: Serum enzyme activity rises from release, increased production (osteoblast ALP in growing children) or reduced clearance (macroenzymes); routine measurements cannot distinguish a macroenzyme from the normal enzyme.
Macroenzyme definition, prevalence, common enzymes, benign nature, PEG screening with laboratory-specific limits.
Macroamylase IgA ~70%/IgG ~30%; clearance ↓ ≥100-fold; normal lipase, low clearance ratio, gel filtration gold standard.

The reference CK method measures ATP formed from creatine phosphate and ADP via a hexokinase/G6PD coupled reaction; red-cell adenylate kinase (ATP + AMP ⇌ 2 ADP) falsely raises CK and CK-MB despite AMP and diadenosine pentaphosphate; haemolysis raises LD and AST.
Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed from two of three criteria (pain, amylase or lipase above three times the upper limit, imaging); lipase is the preferred marker.
EDTA chelates divalent ions; contamination lowers ALP, CK, amylase, calcium, magnesium and raises potassium; AST/ALT barely affected.

The Oliver–Rosalki eponym; macroenzyme ~3-week IgG-like half-life; citrate/oxalate and calcium as a CK cofactor; zinc as the ALP cofactor; renin exception; renal failure raising amylase/lipase; bile-salt release of ALP/GGT; GGT rise from enzyme induction by ethanol; “unmeasurably low” ALP.
claims.note: Not taught; not confirmed in sources read. Kalas 2021 reports GGT raised with cytochrome-inducing medications and alcohol but does not give the mechanism. Radišić Biljak 2025 states the IFCC CK reagent contains EDTA to bind Ca2+, which argues against calcium as a CK cofactor (flag f-ck-calcium-cofactor). The IFCC CK method paper (Hørder 1990) could not be read (no full text; PDF blocked).

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 21 Hit 4 describes macroenzymes as enzyme–autoantibody complexes with an IgG-like half-life of about 3 weeks. Dedeene 2023 describes complexes with immunoglobulins or lipoproteins or self-polymerisation, and Čásenská 2023 reports macroamylase is typically IgA (70%) and less often IgG (30%); the ~3-week half-life was not found in the sources read (register flag rv-macroenzyme-composition).

Ch. 21 Exam Trap 2 (and a Memory Hook) says citrate lowers CK by stripping its calcium cofactor. Radišić Biljak 2025, describing the IFCC reference CK method, states the reaction mixture contains EDTA to bind Ca2+ ions, so calcium is not presented as a CK cofactor there; the lesson does not teach calcium as a CK cofactor (register flag rv-ck-calcium-cofactor).
